activities.anchor: Multiplying rate × time only works when the rate is constant
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the accumulation operation
activities.name: intIdeaCloze

config.text: Multiplying rate × time only works when the rate is constant; the instant it varies, you must add up the contributions of infinitely many %%0%% constant moments. That 'add up the infinitely many thin slices' operation is the %%1%%.
config.hint: Each slice holds the rate still for a moment; the elongated S names the whole operation.

activities.anchor: The true answer is squeezed between them
activities.caption: call the squeeze target
activities.name: intSliceEst

config.prompt: Four right-edge strips under x² from 0 to 1 give ≈ 0.469; left edges give 0.219. In the limit of infinitely thin strips, both meet at what value?
config.why: Exactly ⅓ — that limiting value is the definite integral ∫₀¹ x² dx, and the two-sided squeeze is the proof that it exists for any continuous function.
config.context: right sum overcounts on a rising function, left sum undercounts

activities.anchor: A business losing money for a quarter
activities.caption: true or false — signed area in the ledger
activities.name: intSignedJudge

config.statement: A business losing money for a quarter contributes a positive amount to the annual total when its profit-flow is integrated over the year.
config.why: A negative rate subtracts from the total — to get genuine geometric area you must integrate |f|, splitting the interval at every crossing of the axis.

activities.anchor: Two standard cases sit outside the power rule
activities.caption: file each integral under its route
activities.name: intPowerSort

config.prompt: File each integral under the rule that solves it:

items.label: ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C
∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C — its own anti-derivative

config.why: Raise the power by one, divide by the new power — the two exceptions are worth memorising as counterparts of the derivative table.

config.prompt: One of these claims about the +C is wrong — click it:
lines: Derivatives destroy constants: x² + 3 and x² − 7 both differentiate to 2x.
Reversing recovers only the shape, not the height.
The family x³/3 + C shares one slope.
In a definite integral the +C must be found from a boundary condition first.
config.correction: In a definite integral the constants cancel between the top and bottom limits — no +C is needed.
config.why: A boundary condition picks the one member of the family that fits reality, but the definite integral never needs it.

activities.caption: two ways to evaluate one integral — drag the divider
activities.name: intFtcCompare

before.label: slicing
before.text: sum f(x)·dx over infinitely many strips — a limit of slice sums

after.label: Fundamental Theorem
after.text: find any anti-derivative F and compute F(b) − F(a) — the constant cancels

config.why: The theorem converts a problem about infinite sums into a problem about reversing the rules you already know — and here both give 14.

activities.anchor: Three properties follow directly from "slices add up"
activities.caption: pair each property with its statement
activities.name: intPropMatch

config.prompt: Pair each integral property with its statement:

pairs.right: swapping the limits flips the sign — walking backwards negates every slice

config.why: All three come free from the slice picture — and ∫ₐᵃ = 0: no interval, no accumulation.

activities.anchor: with the line on top in between
activities.caption: call the gap between the curves
activities.name: intAreaEst

config.prompt: Between y = x and y = x², meeting at x = 0 and x = 1, the area is ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx. What is it?
config.why: ½ − ⅓ = 1/6 — the same subtraction is how economists compute consumer surplus and pharmacokinetics compares drug concentrations.

config.prompt: Rebuild the substitution for ∫ 2x·(x² + 1)³ dx — what comes first:
items: Spot an inner function whose derivative also appears outside
Set u = x² + 1 with du = 2x·dx sitting right there
Differentiate back to check — the chain rule restores the 2x
config.why: Roughly: 'match the inside, grab its derivative' — substitution is the chain rule run in reverse.

activities.anchor: joins them with parabolas and is startlingly accurate
activities.caption: drop the marker — Simpson's error gain
activities.name: intSimpsonPlace

config.prompt: Simpson's rule error shrinks with the fourth power of the strip width. Halve the strips and the error improves by what factor?
config.why: 16× — for ∫₀¹ e^(−x²) dx, four parabola-width strips already give five-decimal accuracy against the true value 0.7468.
